did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with the heading “For the leader, a psalm of David,” indicating that it is a psalm intended for musical performance or direction and, according to the heading, attributed to David.
At the very beginning of the psalm, trust and supplication appear together: the psalmist says, “In you, Lord, I take refuge,” and in the same verse asks to be saved “in your righteousness.”
The psalmist uses several images of protection: the Lord is for him a “strong rock,” a “fortified house,” “my rock,” and “my fortress”—images of a stable, secure place protected from danger.
The verse “Into your hand I entrust my spirit” expresses the surrender of the self and one’s life to the Lord’s care; immediately afterward, the Lord is described as the “God of truth.”
The psalmist emphasizes that the Lord is not only a future savior but also sees present distress: “You have seen my affliction; you have known the troubles of my soul.”
At the center of the psalm, a crisis affecting both body and soul is described: the psalmist’s eyes, soul, and body are weakening, and he goes on to describe grief, sighing, and failing strength.

The feeling of social rejection is portrayed through two powerful images: “I am forgotten like someone dead, out of mind,” and “I have become like a lost vessel”—someone whom others no longer notice or care about.
Despite describing persecution and fear, the psalmist returns to a clear declaration of trust: “But I trust in you, Lord; I say, ‘You are my God.’”
The expression “My times are in your hand” presents the psalmist’s times and circumstances as being in the Lord’s hands. From this comes his request to be rescued from his enemies and persecutors.

The psalmist describes a change from panic to an answer of faith: in his haste, he thought he had been cut off from the Lord’s sight, but afterward he recognized that the Lord had heard the voice of his pleas.

The conclusion addresses all who wait for the Lord: “Be strong, and let your hearts be courageous.” In this way, the psalm moves from describing the psalmist’s personal distress to offering public encouragement to all who await the Lord’s salvation.
